cse-2016-1-cs-35.approach: Trace the recursion keeping one shared copy of the static variable $d$: the "pre" prints happen while descending and the final prints happen while unwinding, after every increment is already done.

steps.title: Static means one shared d
steps.body: \`static int d=1\` is initialised once, before the first call. All three activations of \`count\` read and write the **same** $d$.

steps.title: Descending phase
steps.body:
- \`count(3)\`: prints $3$, $d=1$ → prints \`3 1\`, then $d=2$.
- \`count(2)\`: prints \`2 2\`, then $d=3$.
- \`count(1)\`: prints \`1 3\`, then $d=4$; $n>1$ is false, so no further call.

steps.title: Unwinding phase
steps.body:
Now each of the three activations executes its last \`printf("%d ", d)\`. By now $d=4$ and it never changes again, so \`4\` is printed three times (by \`count(1)\`, \`count(2)\`, \`count(3)\`).

Output: \`3 1 2 2 1 3 4 4 4\` → **(A)**.

Treats d as an ordinary local re-initialised to 1 on each call; static variables are initialised only once.

\`n(a)\` passes m's $a$ by reference, so $x$ aliases m's $a$. In \`n\`, the free name $a$ is resolved dynamically, i.e. to the caller m's $a$, which is $2$.

$x = x \times a = 2 \times 2 = 4$. This also sets m's $a = 4$ (alias). It prints **4**.

cse-2016-1-cs-37.approach: Move the last element into position $i$ and restore the heap by moving it either up or down; either way it travels along one root-to-leaf path, which has at most $d$ edges.

steps.title: Delete in O(1)
steps.body: Copy the last array element $A[n]$ into $A[i]$ and shrink the heap by one. Only position $i$ may now break the heap property.

steps.title: Re-fix along one path
steps.body: If the new $A[i]$ is better than its parent, sift **up** (at most $d$ swaps, towards the root); otherwise sift **down** (at most $d$ swaps, towards a leaf). Each swap is $O(1)$, so the fix costs $O(d)$.

steps.title: Why not O(1)
steps.body: In the worst case (e.g. $i$ is the root and the moved element is the smallest in a max-heap) the element sinks all $d$ levels, so the bound $O(d)$ is tight and the cost is not $O(1)$ → **(B)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Removal itself is O(1), but the moved element may have to sift across all d levels.
Correct: one sift-up or sift-down along a path of at most d edges, and the worst case really needs d swaps.
2^d is about the number of nodes; re-heapifying never needs to touch the whole heap.
d·2^d is like rebuilding with repeated sifts, which is unnecessary.

pitfalls: Thinking only sift-down is needed: a replacement taken from another subtree may need to move up.
Confusing depth d with the number of nodes n ≈ 2^d.
cse-2016-1-cs-37.verification: Since n ≤ 2^(d+1) − 1, O(d) = O(log n), the familiar cost of heap deletion.

cse-2016-1-cs-38.approach: Edge $\{3,4\}$ (weight $x$) lies on a shortest path only if it is no longer than the shortest alternative route between its own endpoints; find that alternative distance.

steps.title: Key observation
steps.body: If edge $3$–$4$ is on some shortest $u$–$v$ path, then the sub-path $3$–$4$ is itself a shortest $3$–$4$ path. So we need $x \le d'(3,4)$, where $d'$ is the shortest $3$–$4$ distance avoiding that edge.

steps.title: Largest x
steps.body: For $x = 12$ the direct edge ties with the best detour, so the edge itself is a shortest $3$–$4$ path. For $x = 13$ the detour (12) is strictly shorter, and no other pair can benefit either (any path through the edge could be shortcut by the detour). Answer: **12**.

cse-2016-1-cs-39.approach: Kruskal always takes edges 1 and 2 (two edges cannot form a cycle). To make the MST heavy, make edge 3 useless by closing a triangle with 1 and 2; then the cheapest remaining edge, 4, must connect the fourth vertex.

steps.title: Edges 1 and 2 are always taken
steps.body: An MST on 4 vertices has 3 edges. Kruskal picks the lightest edges first; edges 1 and 2 can never form a cycle, so both are always in the MST.

steps.title: Waste edge 3
steps.body: Put weights 1, 2, 3 on a triangle $A$–$B$–$C$. Then edge 3 closes a cycle and is rejected. The fourth vertex $D$ has edges 4, 5, 6 (to $A$, $B$, $C$).

steps.title: Third edge
steps.body:
Kruskal now takes edge 4 (to $D$). MST weight $= 1 + 2 + 4 = 7$.

It cannot be more: of the edges $\{3,4\}$, at most one can be rejected (edges 1, 2, 3 can form only one cycle), so the third MST edge weighs at most 4. Answer: **7**.

pitfalls: Answering 1 + 2 + 3 = 6, the minimum possible MST weight, instead of the maximum.
Trying to also waste edge 4: edges 1, 2, 3, 4 on 4 vertices cannot all lie in triangles that exclude both 3 and 4.
cse-2016-1-cs-39.verification: If both 3 and 4 were rejected, each would join two vertices already linked by edges 1 and 2, which span only 3 vertices; that triangle has just one free pair, so 3 and 4 would be parallel edges — impossible. Hence the third edge is at most 4 and 7 is the maximum.

cse-2016-1-cs-40.approach: Check each statement against the cycle property (the unique heaviest edge of a cycle is in no MST) and build a tiny counterexample for I.

steps.title: Statement II is true
steps.body: Cycle property: let $e$ be the heaviest edge of some cycle $C$ (weights distinct). If an MST $T$ contained $e$, deleting $e$ splits $T$ into two parts; some other edge $f$ of $C$ reconnects them, and $w(f) < w(e)$, so $T - e + f$ is lighter — contradiction. Hence every MST excludes $e$.

steps.title: Statement I is false
steps.body:
Take 4 vertices with edges $AB=1$, $BC=2$, $CA=3$, $AD=4$, $CD=5$.

- Cycle $A$–$C$–$D$: weights $3, 5, 4$; the lightest is $CA = 3$.
- But $CA = 3$ is the heaviest edge of cycle $A$–$B$–$C$ (weights $1, 2, 3$), so by II it is in **no** MST (MST $= \{AB, BC, AD\}$, weight 7).

So "lightest edge of some cycle" does not force inclusion.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: Only II holds → **(B)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: I is false (counterexample above) and II is true, so "I only" is wrong on both counts.
Correct: II is exactly the cycle property; I fails when e is also the heaviest edge of another cycle.
I is false.
II is true (cycle property).

pitfalls: Confusing I with the cut property: the lightest edge across some cut is in every MST, but being lightest on a cycle is a different, weaker condition.
cse-2016-1-cs-40.verification: In the example, Kruskal takes AB(1), BC(2), rejects CA(3) (cycle), takes AD(4): MST {AB, BC, AD} excludes CA although CA is lightest in cycle A–C–D.

cse-2016-1-cs-41.approach: Each element can be pushed and popped many times. The worst case is when every element has to be cycled back through the queue as often as possible; charging iterations per element gives at most $n^2$, and a reverse-sorted queue reaches it.

steps.title: What the loop does
steps.body: An iteration either moves the queue head onto the stack (when the stack top is $\le$ head) or moves the stack top back to the rear of the queue. The loop ends when every number sits on the stack in non-decreasing order (bottom → top).

scene.caption: n = 3 sorted on the stack after 9 = 3² iterations

steps.title: General bound
steps.body:
Exhaustive simulation over all orderings for $n = 1, \dots, 7$ gives a maximum of $1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49$ iterations, i.e. $n^2$, and a reverse-sorted queue of length $n$ attains $n^2$.

For $n = 16$: $16^2 = $ **256**.

Answering 2n² by counting push and pop of the same element as separate full passes.
cse-2016-1-cs-41.verification: Simulated the loop exhaustively for n ≤ 7 (max = n²) and directly on a reverse-sorted queue of 16 numbers: exactly 256 iterations.

cse-2016-1-cs-43.approach: Read the PDA: it pushes one $X$ per $a$, pops one $X$ per $b$, and accepts at the start state (any $a^n$) or at the final state once the stack is back to $Z$ (exactly $a^n b^n$). Every move is forced, so the PDA is deterministic.

steps.title: What is accepted
steps.body:
- In $q_0$ each $a$ pushes an $X$. $q_0$ is accepting, so every $a^n$ ($n \ge 0$, including $\varepsilon$) is accepted.
- The first $b$ (needs top $X$) moves to $q_1$; each further $b$ pops one $X$.
- When the stack top is $Z$ again (as many $b$'s as $a$'s), $\varepsilon, Z/Z$ moves to accepting $q_2$.

So $L = \{a^n \mid n \ge 0\} \cup \{a^n b^n \mid n \ge 0\}$.

steps.title: It is deterministic
steps.body: In every (state, input, top) at most one move applies: $q_0$ reads $a$ or $b$ (on top $X$); in $q_1$, $b$ needs top $X$ while the $\varepsilon$-move needs top $Z$, so they never compete. Hence a DPDA accepts $L$ and $L$ is a **deterministic CFL** → **(D)**.

| Stack | Input | Action | Print |

| (empty) | a a b | shift a | |
| a | a b | shift a | |
| a a | b | reduce $S \to a$ | 2 |
| a S | b | shift b | |
| a S b | (end) | reduce $A \to Sb$ | 3 |
| a A | (end) | reduce $S \to aA$ | 1 |
| S | (end) | accept | |

steps.title: Table size
steps.body: Each entry $= 48$ bits $= 6$ B. Size $= 2^{26} \times 6\text{ B} = 6 \times 64\text{ MB} = 384$ MB. Answer: **384**.

cse-2016-1-cs-48.approach: C-LOOK sweeps upward to the highest pending request, jumps straight to the lowest pending request, and sweeps upward again; add the three distances.
cse-2016-1-cs-48.given: Head at 63 moving up. Requests sorted: 10, 11, 38, 47, **63**, 87, 92, 121, 191.

steps.title: Jump back

cse-2016-1-cs-49.approach: Simulate both policies on the two passes over $a_1..a_{20}$. First pass: 20 compulsory faults either way. Second pass: count how many of the 10 resident pages are still useful.

steps.title: LIFO
steps.body:
First pass: $a_1..a_{10}$ fill the frames (10 faults). Each of $a_{11}..a_{20}$ faults and replaces the most recently loaded page, so the same frame is overwritten each time (10 more faults). Frames now: $a_1..a_9, a_{20}$.

Second pass: $a_1..a_9$ hit; $a_{10}$ faults (replaces $a_{20}$), and so does each of $a_{11}..a_{20}$ → 11 faults.

LIFO total $= 20 + 11 = 31$.

steps.title: Optimal
steps.body:
First pass: 20 faults (all distinct). After it, OPT keeps 10 pages that are all used again in the second pass, so in the second pass 10 references hit and only the other 10 pages fault (each replaces a page already used for the last time).

OPT total $= 20 + 10 = 30$.

steps.title: Difference
steps.body: LIFO faults − OPT faults $= 31 - 30 = $ **1**. The extra fault arises because LIFO ends pass 1 holding $a_{20}$, which is needed only at the very end, so pass 2 faults on 11 pages ($a_{10}, \dots, a_{20}$) instead of 10.

pitfalls: Assuming OPT avoids misses on the first pass — the first 20 references are all compulsory misses.
Forgetting that LIFO also evicts a_20, so a_10 through a_20 (11 pages) fault on the second pass.
cse-2016-1-cs-49.verification: Simulated both policies on the 40-reference string with 10 frames: LIFO 31 faults, OPT 30 faults.

cse-2016-1-cs-50.approach: This is Lamport's bakery algorithm without the tie-break on process id. The waiting loop still prevents two processes from being in the CS together, but two processes holding equal tickets wait on each other forever.

steps.title: Mutual exclusion holds
steps.body: For $P_i$ to enter, for every $j$ either $t[j] = 0$ or $t[j] > t[i]$ (after $P_j$ finished choosing, guaranteed by \`while (c[j])\`). If $P_i$ and $P_j$ were both in the CS, we would need $t[j] > t[i]$ and $t[i] > t[j]$ — impossible (with equal tickets neither gets in). So at most one process is in the CS → (A) true.

steps.title: Deadlock is possible
steps.body: $P_0$ and $P_1$ compute \`pmax\` at the same time, both see all zeros, and both get $t = 1$. Now $P_0$ waits while $t[1] = 1 \le t[0] = 1$, and $P_1$ waits while $t[0] = 1 \le t[1] = 1$. Neither ever proceeds: a deadlock, so D is false.

steps.title: Progress and bounded wait fail
steps.body: In that state the CS is free but no one can enter, so progress fails; the processes wait forever, so bounded waiting fails too. Only **(A)** is TRUE.

answer.value: At most one process can be in the critical section at any time

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: two processes in the CS would need t[i] < t[j] and t[j] < t[i] at once.
Equal tickets make both processes wait forever, so waiting is not bounded.
With equal tickets the CS is empty yet nobody can enter, violating progress.
Equal tickets (no (ticket, id) tie-break) cause exactly such a deadlock.

pitfalls: Assuming it is the full bakery algorithm, which breaks ties using the process index.
cse-2016-1-cs-50.verification: The real bakery algorithm compares (t[j], j) < (t[i], i); dropping the index is what allows the equal-ticket deadlock.

cse-2016-1-cs-51.approach: Check two things separately: does the protocol satisfy two-phase locking (serializability), and can a circular wait form when locks are always requested in one global order (deadlock)?

steps.title: Serializable
steps.body: T acquires all its locks (growing phase) before releasing any (shrinking phase), so the protocol is (in fact conservative/strict) 2PL. Every 2PL schedule is conflict serializable.

steps.title: Deadlock-free
steps.body: All transactions request exclusive locks in increasing order of address. A cycle in the wait-for graph would need some transaction to wait for a lower-addressed object while holding a higher one, which never happens. So no circular wait, no deadlock → **(A)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: 2PL gives serializability and global lock ordering removes circular wait.
Both properties hold.
Ordered acquisition prevents deadlock, so "not deadlock-free" is wrong.
All locks are held before any is released (2PL), so serializability is guaranteed.

pitfalls: Remembering only that basic 2PL can deadlock — the fixed acquisition order removes that.
cse-2016-1-cs-51.verification: Same argument as resource ordering for OS deadlock prevention: a total order on resources breaks the circular-wait condition.

cse-2016-1-cs-52.approach: A digital signature is the digest encrypted with the **sender's private** key; anyone can verify it with the sender's public key.

steps.title: Verification
